lines: Pay attention to what's actually being asked for here, because it's a harder question than it looks.
Everything you had before could always produce some order between two versions, right or wrong.
What you need now is the honest ability to say there is no order at all, and still keep both.
Before you pick, think about what comparing two versions is actually checking.
It isn't checking which has the bigger total. It's checking whether one truly contains every change the other made.
answer: Both, and here's the reasoning that makes it certain rather than a guess.
Comparing the two versions entry by entry, neither one's numbers are all at least as large as the other's.
That is exactly what concurrent means, and once that's true, there is no basis left for discarding either side.

lines: Notice how small the actual mechanism is once you strip away the word vector.
Bump your own entry whenever you do something. When you hear from someone else, keep whichever number is bigger, position by position.
One version truly contains another exactly when every single position agrees, and at least one is strictly ahead.
Walk through this as a real trace, not a diagram, because every step is mechanical and that's the whole point.
One coordinator writes, then writes again, each time only touching its own number.
Two other coordinators each branch off that same point, neither one seeing what the other did, and a reconciling write later folds both branches back into one.
Keep the distinction here sharp, because it's easy to blur.
One version of this idea watches events happening at processes. The other watches versions of one specific item sitting at replicas.
The comparison never changes. Only what each entry is counting does.
Separate two different costs here, because people tend to treat them as the same complaint.
Keeping both versions when neither dominates is not a failure. It's the store refusing to guess.
Letting those kept versions multiply forever because nobody ever merges them back is the actual failure, and it's a client problem, not a clock problem.
Watch exactly what breaks when two different people happen to write through the same coordinator.
The coordinator bumps its own number the same way both times, so by the numbers alone, the second write looks like it simply replaced the first.
One small tag, naming the specific event that produced each write, is enough to stop that collapse from happening.
Carry forward what this mechanism actually buys you, stated plainly.
A vector tells concurrency apart from order exactly, which a single number never could.
Keeping both versions when neither wins is the honest choice, and a small tag keeps that honesty from turning into endless duplicates.
Shrinking that vector on purpose, to save space, is a real trade, and it has a real cost.
Before you answer, think about what gets thrown away when old entries are dropped to save space.
Ask whether the proof that one version truly contained another could ever be sitting in exactly the entry that just got discarded.
answer: Yes, and this is worth remembering precisely because it's easy to assume size limits are free.
If the discarded entry was the only one showing the earlier version's history was fully included in the later one, nothing is left to prove that anymore.
The pair now reads as concurrent, even though it never actually was.
